summary:
Mars Route Navigator is an interactive web map that helps astronauts plan a safe, science-rich surface excursion. A user picks a start point and a destination, and the tool returns the best route that avoids steep slopes, rough ground and loose sand or dust. It layers five kinds of NASA data: topographic, optical, thermal, spectral and radiation or atmospheric values. In Science mode, it ranks astrobiologically relevant targets, such as hydrated mineral exposures, and adds the best ones to the route within an adjustable detour budget, while safety limits always take priority. A validator checks every route segment against the obstacle mask, and a helmet-style HUD view shows the next waypoint, slope-ahead warnings, radiation status and the next target.

The tool meets the challenge by combining more than three data types and serving safety and science in one interface. It matters because crews will need hyperlocal maps, not just regional ones. Every value is labeled measured, estimated or assumed, and a data-fidelity badge shows how far each route can be trusted.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Mars Route Navigator is an interactive web map for planning a Mars surface excursion. The user chooses a start point and a destination, and the tool returns the best route that avoids steep slopes, rough ground, cliffs and loose sand or dust. Behind the map, a Python pipeline crops and aligns NASA layers for a site, then builds an obstacle mask from slope, roughness, curvature and a sand and dust proxy. A pathfinding algorithm (A*) searches a time-based cost grid in which obstacles are impassable, and a validator checks every route segment before it is displayed. In Science mode, the tool scores spectral, optical and thermal data to rank astrobiologically relevant targets, then adds the best ones as waypoints within an adjustable detour budget. The user can view the result in a planner view or a simplified helmet-style HUD view, which shows the next waypoint, slope-ahead warnings, radiation status and the next target.

What benefits does it have?

It gives crews one view that combines five kinds of NASA data (topographic, optical, thermal, spectral, and radiation or atmospheric values) instead of switching between separate tools. It serves safety and science together: safety limits are hard rules, and science targets are added only when they fit within those limits. It shows a radiation dose estimate and shelter points. It also makes trust visible. Each route carries a data-fidelity badge, and each value is labeled measured, estimated or assumed. Where only coarse elevation data exists, the tool withholds walking-scale routes instead of guessing.

What is the intended impact?

The aim is to help close the gap between regional Mars maps and the hyperlocal maps that astronauts will need on individual spacewalks. It could support early mission planning, help scientists decide where a crew’s limited time is best spent, and show what additional data would be needed at a candidate site. Because the sites are generated by a pipeline, the same approach could be extended to other Mars locations and, later, other destinations such as the Moon.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Languages: Python and JavaScript, plus HTML and CSS
  • Python libraries: NumPy, SciPy, rasterio and Pillow
  • Web: Leaflet for the interactive map, a Web Worker for in-browser routing
  • Data: NASA datasets (HiRISE, CTX, MOLA or HRSC elevation, THEMIS, CRISM, and Curiosity RAD, REMS and MEDA), accessed through resources such as Mars Trek, USGS Astrogeology and the Planetary Data System
  • Development: AI coding assistants for code generation, with our team checking every coordinate, value and calculation; Git and GitHub for version control and GitHub Pages for hosting
  • Hardware: standard laptops, with no special equipment

How is the project creative?

Most Mars tools show data. This one uses it to make decisions. Its main idea is a dual-purpose route: safety is a fixed limit, science is a value to maximize inside it, and the user can see the trade-off by switching between Direct and Science modes. The fidelity and provenance badges turn data limitations into a visible feature instead of hiding them. The HUD view imagines how the same analysis would look on a spacesuit visor. The site-pack design means a new location needs a pipeline run, not new code.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Astronaut safety first: hard no-go limits, a clearance buffer around obstacles, and a validator that blocks any route through an obstacle.
  • Data honesty: coverage and resolution vary across Mars, so we added a fidelity badge. Dust and sand are shown as proxies, not measurements, and we avoid any claim of biosignature detection.
  • Radiation: solar events can’t be predicted from a map, so we show shelter points and dose budgets, not forecasts.
  • Assumptions: suit, speed and slope values are labeled as assumptions, not NASA specifications.
  • Technical accuracy: Mars radius for distances, one longitude and latitude convention, and tests for coordinate conversion and for routes that cross the 0/360 line.
  • Scope and teamwork: a narrow scope of two test sites, a shared set of file formats, and a clear split of work among four members.
  • Limits: the tool is an illustrative planning aid and is not flight-validated.
